tagline: Two coasts, three resort capitals — Los Cabos, the Riviera Maya and Puerto Vallarta on the water.
summary: Mexico's marine-mobility story runs across three of the world's busiest resort coasts: Los Cabos on the Baja peninsula, the Cancún–Riviera Maya Caribbean belt with its day-islands of Isla Mujeres and Cozumel, and Puerto Vallarta on the Pacific Bay of Banderas. Each is a dense cluster of marinas, resorts and ferry corridors served today by diesel ferries, catamarans and private launches. A clean, fast, stabilised foiling tier is the premium-but-practical layer none of these coasts has yet.
why_marine_mobility: Mexico's coastal demand is concentrated, not dispersed: short, high-volume crossings between resort marinas and day-islands. Cancún and Playa Caracol to Isla Mujeres, the Riviera Maya's Cozumel ferry corridor, Los Cabos' Palmilla–San José del Cabo marina belt, and Puerto Vallarta's Marina Vallarta and Riviera Nayarit hops are all short legs run today on diesel ferries and charter boats. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier flies these crossings smooth, dry, clean and on demand — a direct premium upgrade on routes that already carry millions of passengers.

demand_signals.label: High-end resort & residential gravity
demand_signals.note: Los Cabos, the Riviera Maya and Puerto Vallarta host some of the hemisphere's most concentrated luxury resort and branded-residence development, including Discovery Land Company communities — an affluent, recurring premium-transfer market.

demand_signals.label: Day-island ferry volume
demand_signals.note: The Cancún–Isla Mujeres and Playa del Carmen–Cozumel corridors move very large daily passenger volumes on conventional ferries — captive, high-frequency demand ripe for a clean premium tier.

demand_signals.label: Marina-belt density
demand_signals.note: Each resort cluster concentrates many marinas within a few nautical miles, where land transfers are slow and congested — a natural on-demand marina-to-marina shuttle market.

use_cases.body: Cancún (Playa Caracol) to Isla Mujeres: the marquee Caribbean day-island crossing, flown smooth and dry on Pioneer II as a clean premium alternative to the diesel ferry.

Los Cabos marina belt: Palmilla to the San José del Cabo marina and the Cabo San Lucas corridor — short premium transfers serving the resort-and-residence clientele, including Discovery Land communities, on a clean foiling shuttle.

Puerto Vallarta and the Bay of Banderas: clean, quiet Pioneer II hops between Marina Vallarta, Riviera Nayarit and the bay's beach clubs, matching a high-end leisure market with no comparable water product today.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Every featured leg sits well inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range: the Cancún–Isla Mujeres crossing, the Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta marina belts, and the Riviera Maya day-island corridors are all commercial-ready today at 30 knots — direct, clean substitutes for diesel ferries and charter boats.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer trunks — a Los Cabos-to-La Paz Baja run, or a Caribbean coastal line-haul beyond day-island range — are Quanta-LR corridors (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), opening legs no battery day-boat can serve.

signature_routes.label: Cancún (Playa Caracol) ↔ Isla Mujeres — the marquee Caribbean day-island crossing
Los Cabos — Palmilla ↔ San José del Cabo Marina
Puerto Vallarta / Riviera Nayarit — Bay of Banderas marina leg
Playa del Carmen ↔ Cozumel — the iconic Caribbean ferry corridor (no network leg yet)

transit_planning: For a marina operator, resort group or ferry concessionaire: a clean, fast, on-demand water tier layered onto coasts that already move millions by boat. Start with the proven high-volume day-island and marina-belt hops on Pioneer II — riding existing berths and ferry docks with no new infrastructure — then extend to longer Baja and Caribbean coastal trunks on Quanta-LR as range comes online. The Cozumel corridor is an obvious next leg once a network route is established.
competitive_landscape: Mexico's resort coasts run on high-volume diesel ferries (UltraMar and others on the Caribbean day-island routes), catamaran day-trips and private launches — reliable and affordable, but diesel, fixed-schedule and unremarkable. There is no clean, on-demand premium tier. Navier's foiling craft is the missing option: faster and smoother than a ferry, cleaner and quieter than a diesel launch, and matched to a luxury resort market that has no comparable water product today.
regulatory_note: Mexican maritime passenger transport is overseen by SEMAR (the Secretaría de Marina, which now administers the country's ports and harbour-master/capitanía system) and the Secretaría de Infraestructura, Comunicaciones y Transportes; passenger operation requires vessel registration and crew certification. State tourism authorities in Baja California Sur, Quintana Roo and Jalisco/Nayarit are natural first touchpoints.
seasonality: Peak demand runs the dry winter high season (Nov–Apr) with the calmest Caribbean and Pacific conditions; the summer–autumn hurricane season (roughly Jun–Nov, peak Sep) brings heavier weather and ferry disruption to both coasts — the window where a stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule when conventional craft cannot.

precedents.what: Four Seasons Lake Austin operates an N30 in live luxury-hospitality service — proof of the premium resort water-shuttle model Navier brings to Mexico's resort coasts.
